newsitem.title: UK: Polish c.bank chief sees no rate cut soon.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank chief sees no rate cut soon.

text.p: The president of the Polish central bank, Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz, on Tuesday ruled out cutting interest rates soon because credit growth was still too high.

But she refused to make any forecasts on what might happen in two to threee months, saying this depended on the trend in credit growth, which has risen sharply for both corporate and consumer borrowers last year and this.
Speaking in an interview, she also told Reuters that she could not rule out another rise in compulsory minimum reserve requirements for commercial banks if the lending boom continued.
Real interest rates have actually risen in Poland as inflation has fallen to 16.6 percent year-on-year in March from 20.4 a year earlier while nominal rates have remained unchanged.
But this has had little affect on credit expansion as banks increasingly compete with each other for lending business.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz, who is attending the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London, noted that interest rates were now about five percentage points over inflation. "Interest rates depend on inflation and credit growth. Both are too high now," she said.
"I don't think that we could cut interest rates soon. This I can exclude," she said. "But you can never know what will happen in two or three months. In our case that's quite long-term."

She also played down the chances of any early cut in the devaluation rate of the zloty. Under a "crawling peg" policy, the currency is devalued by one percent a month to compensate for inflation which is higher than in major trading partners.

According to this year's budget, the zloty should be devalued only nine percent. Such targets have been overshot in past years due to too high inflation and Gronkiewicz-Waltz said this year's target was only approximate.

In March the National Bank of Poland increased the minimum reserve requirement, whereby commercial banks have to deposit compulsory reserves with the central bank, to 20 percent for short-term deposits and nine percent for long-term.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said minimum reserve requirements were a more direct tool for lowering credit growth than interest rates.
Asked if the National Bank might raise them again, she said: "Yes, it depends on credit growth. It cannot be excluded."

The rapid expansion of consumer credit, albeit from a low base, has attracted wide publicity. But Gronkiewicz-Waltz said: "My concern is not only consumer credit but also corporate credit which grew 35 percent last year."
